author: KAASHVI SHARMA Staff Reporter
title: Purdue club modifies toys for kids with disabilities - NewsBreak
text:
By KAASHVI SHARMA Staff Reporter ,
8 hours ago The Adapted Toys for Children club at Purdue makes toys custom-made for disabled children. They utilize CAD skills, soldering, and other technical skills basic to the engineering field. ATC has bi-weekly meetings, from 6:30-8:30 p.m. on Tuesdays in Dudley Hall, Room 5369.
This club is specific to Purdue and is open to anyone interested in working with basic circuit boards, regardless of major.
Members in the club get to choose from a multitude of toys to tinker with, modify, and eventually give to local elementary school students with disabilities. One toy, aimed to teach kids about the alphabet, had small parts that proved to be difficult to use for kids with disabilities that cause them to lack motor control. After modifying, the toy was given bigger buttons, allowing for easier use.
The practical use of the toys is straightforward and aims to help kids with motor problems, such as difficulty using switches and smaller toy parts. Zachary Schreiber, a lecturer in the Polytechnic Institute, also assists club members with toy development.
Kids with wheelchairs especially benefit from ATC’s select use of bigger buttons, often having to pay for expensive modifications from other toy companies. Each semester the club builds around 10-15 toys to give to the children in need.
Each toy's development differs in the way that members have to “take it apart (and) try (to) figure out where the actual buttons lead to on the circuit board”, ATC President Grace Yoder said. The development process otherwise for each toy is very similar, including taking apart the toy, planning button placement, soldering wires, then eventually reassembling the toy.
“You get more hands-on experience with the actual making part, like soldering, which you don't often get in labs,” Yoder said. Creative control is welcomed as well, allowing members to eventually specialize in areas they find interesting, such as 3D printing or sewing to further modify the toys.
Members not only do good for the youth in the Greater Lafayette community, but express that the development process of the toys is enjoyable. “(I) actually (found) walking around… helping people when they get stuck to be very satisfying,” Yoder said.
Team members do not work on the individual toys in a group, “all working separately, but we're all in parallel. We're all doing the same thing,” Yoder said. The peer-to-peer nature of the club fosters a welcoming and exciting environment where members can build not only toys, but their own technical skills.
